In this task, you will evaluate whether each statement is supported by its corresponding citations. Note
that the system responses may appear very fluent and well-formed, but contain slight inaccuracies that are
not easy to discern at first glance. Pay close attention to the text.

You will be provided with a statement and its corresponding passage which the statement cites. It may be
helpful to ask yourself whether it is accurate to say “according to the citation ...” with the statement following this phrase. Be sure to check all of the information in the statement. You will be given three options:

• Full Support: All of the information in the statement is supported in the citation.
• Partial Support: Some parts of the information are supported in the citation, but other parts are missing.
• No Support: The citation does not support any part of the statement.

Please provide your response based on the information in the citation. If you are unsure, use your best
judgment. Respond as either “Full Support”, “Partial Support”, or “No Support” with no additional
information.
Statement: CD earnings are not taxed until the funds are withdrawn, making them a tax‑efficient vehicle for short‑term savings goals.
Citation: Earnings or returns on the CD are tax-exempt until you eventually withdraw the funds for retirement.
Contributions you make to a Roth IRA CD are not tax deductible, but the earnings are tax-free.
Who Can Issue CDs?
CDs are typically offered by banks and credit unions, however, you can also purchase them through brokerage firms or individual brokerage reps referred to as deposit brokers.
Brokerage CDs have a higher annual percentage yield (APY) than bank CDs and much longer terms. You may need to wait 10 to 20 years, or more, for the CD maturity date.
Are CDs Considered Assets?
Yes, a CD is considered an asset that is held by the issuing financial institution.
While the bank holds the CD, it gives the owner — CD purchaser — a specific amount of interest if the CD is invested for a set period of time, as per the CD's term lengths.
A CD is designed to be a stable, short-term cash investment. Bank-purchased CDs are backed by the federal government, and covered by Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) insurance for up to $250,000.
Can You Lose Money Invested in a CD?
That's unlikely. CDs are a low-risk investment product and they do not fluctuate in value. Bank-purchased CDs are FDIC-insured, and credit union CDs have NCUA insurance coverage.
You can, however, lose interest if you withdraw bank or credit union-issued CD funds before their maturity date. Additionally, you may pay an early withdrawal penalty if you withdraw CD funds within a certain date of the account's opening.
Brokerage firms, not member FDIC, may offer other high-yield CDs. These CDs are generally riskier, but brokerage accounts do offer Securities Investment Protector Corporation (SIPC) insurance.
Is Putting Money in a CD Worth It?
In many instances, yes. CDs usually offer much higher interest rates than savings accounts and savings bonds, and they can also outperform many money market accounts (MMAs).
Additionally, the best CD rates can outpace the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and may be a good hedge against inflation.
This means a CD may be worthwhile if you're trying to save for a specific short-term goal, like a house down payment or a new car. And they can also help you meet retirement goals. CDs are commonly part of the investment mix for a low-risk, traditional IRA portfolio.
An accountant or tax professional can help you weigh out the pros and cons of your personal situation to determine whether or not CDs are worth it

Question: Are CDs considered assets? Answer: Yes, they are considered assets held by the issuing financial institution.

Question: Who can issue CDs? Answer: Banks, credit unions, brokerage firms, and deposit brokers.

Question: Can CDs help hedge against inflation? Answer: Yes, the best CD rates can outpace the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

</file>

In this task, you will evaluate whether each statement is supported by its corresponding citations. Note
that the system responses may appear very fluent and well-formed, but contain slight inaccuracies that are
not easy to discern at first glance. Pay close attention to the text.

You will be provided with a statement and its corresponding passage which the statement cites. It may be
helpful to ask yourself whether it is accurate to say “according to the citation ...” with the statement following this phrase. Be sure to check all of the information in the statement. You will be given three options:

• Full Support: All of the information in the statement is supported in the citation.
• Partial Support: Some parts of the information are supported in the citation, but other parts are missing.
• No Support: The citation does not support any part of the statement.

Please provide your response based on the information in the citation. If you are unsure, use your best
judgment. Respond as either “Full Support”, “Partial Support”, or “No Support” with no additional
information.
Statement: CD earnings are not taxed until the funds are withdrawn, making them a tax‑efficient vehicle for short‑term savings goals.
Citation: Earnings or returns on the CD are tax-exempt until you eventually withdraw the funds for retirement.
Contributions you make to a Roth IRA CD are not tax deductible, but the earnings are tax-free.
Who Can Issue CDs?
CDs are typically offered by banks and credit unions, however, you can also purchase them through brokerage firms or individual brokerage reps referred to as deposit brokers.
Brokerage CDs have a higher annual percentage yield (APY) than bank CDs and much longer terms. You may need to wait 10 to 20 years, or more, for the CD maturity date.
Are CDs Considered Assets?
Yes, a CD is considered an asset that is held by the issuing financial institution.
While the bank holds the CD, it gives the owner — CD purchaser — a specific amount of interest if the CD is invested for a set period of time, as per the CD's term lengths.
A CD is designed to be a stable, short-term cash investment. Bank-purchased CDs are backed by the federal government, and covered by Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) insurance for up to $250,000.
Can You Lose Money Invested in a CD?
That's unlikely. CDs are a low-risk investment product and they do not fluctuate in value. Bank-purchased CDs are FDIC-insured, and credit union CDs have NCUA insurance coverage.
You can, however, lose interest if you withdraw bank or credit union-issued CD funds before their maturity date. Additionally, you may pay an early withdrawal penalty if you withdraw CD funds within a certain date of the account's opening.
Brokerage firms, not member FDIC, may offer other high-yield CDs. These CDs are generally riskier, but brokerage accounts do offer Securities Investment Protector Corporation (SIPC) insurance.
Is Putting Money in a CD Worth It?
In many instances, yes. CDs usually offer much higher interest rates than savings accounts and savings bonds, and they can also outperform many money market accounts (MMAs).
Additionally, the best CD rates can outpace the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and may be a good hedge against inflation.
This means a CD may be worthwhile if you're trying to save for a specific short-term goal, like a house down payment or a new car. And they can also help you meet retirement goals. CDs are commonly part of the investment mix for a low-risk, traditional IRA portfolio.
An accountant or tax professional can help you weigh out the pros and cons of your personal situation to determine whether or not CDs are worth it
